newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ruling coalition leads in campaign - poll.
newsitem.headline: French ruling coalition leads in campaign - poll.

text.p: The ruling centre-right has a clear lead in France's parliamentary election race despite mounting disaffection with Prime Minister Alain Juppe, an opinion poll showed on Thursday.

The Ipsos survey, for the weekly magazine Le Point, projected the ruling coalition would win a clear majority with 323 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, up from a wafer-thin majority with 290 in a similar poll last week.

It indicated the opposition Socialists would trail on 226 seats ahead of the Communist Party on 27. The far-right National Front would squeeze into parliament with one seat in the May 25-June 1 election.
Surveys by other polling institutes have shown even clearer leads for the centre-right in recent days despite dismay at record unemployment, sputtering economic growth and political sleaze.

The Ipsos poll also showed that 67 percent of voters wanted President Jacques Chirac to drop Juppe and name a new prime minister if his coalition won, little changed from 65 percent at the end of April.

Just 16 percent of the 1,633 people interviewed on May 13 and 14 wanted Juppe to stay on, down from 19 percent, if he becomes the first sitting prime minister since 1978 to lead his coalition to victory in the National Assembly.

Asked to choose between outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and former prime minister Edouard Balladur as possible alternatives to Juppe, 45 percent favoured Seguin against 31 percent for Balladur.
Underscoring voters' ambiguity, the poll showed that just 37 percent wanted the current coalition to win, the least enthusiastic figure since Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on April 21.

Yet 50 percent thought the coalition would win, up from 45 percent last week. Many voters do not yet trust the Socialists, hit by a right-wing landslide at the last election in 1993 amid rising joblessness and political corruption.
